blocks.text: …Staying calm and conveying calm

Conflicts between our dog and other people are often based on misunderstandings or wrong actions – a conflict rarely originates with the dog. In the rarest of cases does our dog want conflict – usually it is a sum of wrong actions that causes the situation to escalate.

Both cases – defensive and offensive – build on the same basic principles: create distance, enable safety, confirm positively. The difference lies in safety management and in the pace of the approach.
Collecting good, peaceful experiences and avoiding pressure and unpleasantness from other people are the key strategies.
What you should know 📋
During a situation, the potential for conflict can build up and subside extremely quickly. Situations involving conflict rarely develop in a linear or predictable way.
Dogs that have had many bad experiences with people in their lives tend to distrust people and avoid them. In confrontational situations with no way to escape, conflicts then inevitably occur.
Calm handling and de-escalating strategies are the foundation for positive imprinting in a dog that reacts problematically on contact with other people.
Characteristics and body-language signals 👁️

Characteristic: Retreating behaviour and, when cornered, self-defence behaviour such as showing teeth, growling and barking while cowering and evading at the same time. Forward defence through a defensive bite only as a last resort when there is no possibility of escape.

Relaxation signals show: The dog has accepted the situation. In general they go along with calm breathing, a soft gaze with decreasing focus, loose movement and a relaxed posture. Only then is confirmation through play or a treat effective.

Tension signals – body tense, gaze fixed, mouth closed and pressed shut, breathing shallow or held – show: We are still too close, too fast, or the situation has not yet been resolved. The rule here: increase the distance, stay calm, wait.
The role of uninvolved third parties – instructing passers-by 🗣️

One of the most common sources of unintended escalation is well-meant but wrong reactions from passers-by: addressing the dog too directly, approaching quickly, bending down to eye level or holding out hands.
We instruct third parties briefly, clearly and in a friendly manner: “Please just ignore him and carry on walking as normal – that helps him most.” This one sentence is enough in almost all cases.
Anyone who wishes to, and where the situation allows, may place a treat in front of the dog and walk on – for our dog this is the ideal form of a positive first encounter with strangers.
We make this request confidently, in a friendly manner and very calmly. Our dog observes how we deal with other people – that is training too.
Training 🦮
We make absolutely sure that all encounters between people and dog take place in a stress-free and calm atmosphere. The dog is held neither on a short leash nor by the collar.
On a long leash – and better still running free – he should be allowed to decide for himself how far he wants to go into the situation and how close to the person.

At the start of the situation, we guide the dog calmly and in a friendly manner to a safe distance. From this safe distance he may observe what is happening – in order to learn that it is not as threatening as he feared.
If undesired reactions flare up again, we leave the situation calmly and quickly, putting further distance between us, and immediately bring the dog onto a positive level there with play or a treat.
We do not force the dog into situations without necessity, but we also do not pass up any situations that arise to accompany him on his way.
Step-by-step plan – when is the next step ready? 📈
Progress does not come from pressure – but from our dog repeatedly having the experience: closeness to people = nothing bad happens = something good follows.
Step 1 – Observing from a safe distance: Our dog notices people without reacting. We give treats or play. This step is ready to be completed when the dog reliably stays relaxed at this distance.

Step 2 – Reducing the distance: We reduce the distance slowly over several training sessions. The dog sets the pace through his body language. Relaxation signals = continue. Tension signals = back to step 1.
Step 3 – Treat from the ground, placed by third parties: A familiar person calmly places a treat on the ground and walks on – without eye contact. Our dog decides for himself whether to take it.

Step 4 – Treat from the hand of third parties: Only when step 3 works reliably do calm, instructed people offer the treat directly – still without direct eye contact, positioned to the side, not bent over the dog.
Between each step, as much time as necessary may pass. Setbacks are normal – they only show us that we took one step too early.
We remember 🧠
With defensive, retreating fearful behaviour, any coercion or corrective training is to be regarded as reinforcing the problem and must therefore be avoided.
We enable the dog to go to a safe distance – and confirm positively there.
As confidence grows, the distance can be shortened step by step. Relaxation signals in the body language show us when the next step is ready.
Instruct passers-by calmly and briefly: behave neutrally, no direct eye contact, if appropriate place a treat on the ground and walk on.
Always build everything up in small steps. Only positive experiences count as training success!
What you should avoid ⚠️
Avoid coercion, holding the dog and corrective intervention – it reinforces fear.
Avoid speaking loudly to the dog and forcing closeness to people.
Avoid boisterous, overly friendly approaches by third parties – even when well meant, it is counterproductive.
Avoid steps that come too early – setbacks cost more time than patience at the beginning.
Avoid negative experiences caused by wanting too much or by wrong reaction patterns from the person.
Characteristics and own emotional control 🧘

Characteristic: Initially brief retreating behaviour and a rapid switch to surprising offensive actions such as pursuing, jumping up, barking at the person and, under severe pressure, also nipping up to occasional biting. In these situations our dog is barely responsive or not responsive at all.

The offensive dog is the hardest test of our own self-control. Shame, fear of other people's reactions, our own tension – all of this is transferred to the dog immediately and reinforces exactly the behaviour we are trying to reduce.
An effective technique before the first intervention: consciously exhale deeply once, let the shoulders drop, hold the leash loosely. This one moment gives us control back.

In the long term it is worthwhile to reflect calmly afterwards on our own reaction to critical situations: When did I become tense? What did that trigger in the dog? This honesty is a central part of the training.
Training 🦮

We make absolutely sure that all encounters take place at the necessary safety distance in each case. The dog is led through the situation on a leash about 2 metres long. Keeping the leash short is disadvantageous, since for lack of room to move the dog's impression of having to defend himself is reinforced.
People involved behave neutrally at first and stay strictly outside the dog's radius of action (twice the leash length).

The right approach is to train the dog in alternative behaviours to avoid conflict. For this we need toys or treats as well as the content from the training categories Down , Socialisation techniques and Stress tolerance training .

At the start of the situation, we guide the dog calmly and in a friendly manner, on a leash held at full length, quickly to a safe distance and, if possible, bring him into the “down”. From this position he may observe what is happening until the situation has resolved.
We do not force the dog into situations without necessity, but we also do not pass up any situations that arise to accompany him on his way.
Setback management 🔄

Setbacks in offensive fearful behaviour are not an exception – they are a regular part of the learning process. A dog that suddenly escalates again after weeks of progress was overloaded at a moment that we underestimated.

Immediate measure after a setback: leave the situation calmly, stabilise the dog, no escalation through our own agitation. No comment, no scolding. As soon as the dog is calm, praise calmly and end the session.
In the following days: consciously go back to the level last mastered reliably – and build up again from there.

Analysis of causes: Was the distance too small? Was the dog owner tense himself? Were there external stressors? This factual analysis – without self-criticism – helps to avoid repeating the same mistake.
We remember 🧠
With offensive fearful behaviour, purposefully leading the dog to a safe place, followed by “down” or “sit”, is the top priority.
Consciously release our own tension – exhale one breath, let the shoulders drop, hold the leash loosely – before we intervene.
In case of setbacks: step back calmly, analyse the cause factually, build up again from the last stable level.
Build everything up in small steps and with great composure. Only positive experiences count as training success!
What you should avoid ⚠️
Avoid alarmed, agitated behaviour – our restlessness adds directly to the dog's excitement.
Avoid shortening the leash without compelling reason – it reinforces the feeling of confinement and the defensive impulse.
Avoid approaches by third parties within the radius of action (twice the leash length).
Avoid standing still in the situation – leading the dog out quickly and calmly is always the better choice.
Avoid praising too early while the dog is still in a phase of arousal.
Avoid seeking out the same stimulus level again immediately after a setback.
Avoid negative experiences caused by wanting too much – only positive experiences count as training success.
Practical impulse: The one sentence that changes everything

“Please just ignore him and carry on walking as normal – that helps him most.” This one sentence is the most effective tool when dealing with passers-by. Practise it until it comes out without thinking – calmly, in a friendly manner, confidently. Anyone who says this sentence with composure demonstrates to their dog at that moment: I have the situation under control.
→ Do I reliably recognise my dog's relaxation and tension signals?
→ Do I instruct passers-by briefly, calmly and clearly – without a long explanation?
→ Am I training at the level that currently allows my dog safe successful experiences?
→ Do I keep the leash sufficiently long in every phase – no holding on, no shortening?
→ Do I consciously exhale and let my shoulders drop before I intervene in the situation?
→ Do I confirm my dog only after the situation has been completed fully and calmly?
→ In case of setbacks, do I consciously step back and analyse the cause factually?
→ Do I avoid pressure, coercion and forcing closeness in every case?
→ Do I use every situation that arises as a training session – without overwhelming the dog?
→ Only positive experiences count as training success – always!
